paras: The Raleigh street car seat incident took place in Raleigh, North Carolina, around 2 November 1903, when white men seized two Black passengers on a street car at the Fair Grounds and pulled them from their seats after they refused to give the seats up to white college girls. No one was reported hurt, and the only account, in the Raleigh News & Observer, was written to deny a rumor that several Black passengers had been pushed off the car.

The incident followed a football game at the Fair Grounds, where a street car was standing at the grounds. The newspaper did not date the game; its report appeared on 3 November and refers to a rumor that had gone about town the night before.

According to the News & Observer, a number of college girls began to board the car after the game, and most of the men aboard rose to give them their seats while two Black men stayed seated. A "gentleman of this city" asked them twice to get up, and they answered, "No, we don't." "The gentlemen" then seized hold of them and pulled them up from their seats, "and there was an end of the matter," in the paper's words.
No report of an arrest or any official action appears in the coverage.

The News & Observer ran the item under the headline "THERE WAS NO FIGHT" and the subhead "Only Two Negroes Had to Give Up Their Seats to Ladies on Car," presenting its reporter's inquiry as a correction of the rumor. The paper described the men's refusal as the first "act of rudeness in Raleigh by a negro toward white ladies," praised the "polite, respectful conduct" of Raleigh's Black residents, and repeated a gentleman's belief that the two were not from Raleigh. No other white paper and no Black newspaper is known to have reported the incident.

The rumor in town held that several Black passengers had been pushed off the car, while the News & Observer said that only two were pulled from their seats; no independent account settles the difference.

accounts.label: Town rumor
accounts.gist: Several Black passengers had refused to give up their seats to white ladies and had been pushed off the car.

accounts.label: News & Observer reporter's inquiry
accounts.gist: Only two Black men refused; a gentleman asked them twice, and then 'the gentlemen' seized them and pulled them up from their seats, ending the matter.

framing.detail: The News & Observer headlined 'THERE WAS NO FIGHT' and 'Only Two Negroes Had to Give Up Their Seats,' treated the men's refusal as the first 'act of rudeness in Raleigh by a negro toward white ladies,' and suggested they were not Raleigh residents.

versions.value: Several Black passengers pushed off the car (town rumor)
Two Black men pulled up from their seats, not put off the car (reporter's inquiry)

conflicts.note: Both versions appear in the same article; the paper presents its reporter's inquiry as the facts, but no independent account was found.

info: Just after a football game at the Fair Grounds; a rumor of it was going about town on the night before the 3 November 1903 issue (i.e. 2 November), but the article does not date the game itself
A street car standing at the Fair Grounds, Raleigh
Two unnamed Black men ("two negroes"), possibly not from Raleigh according to an unnamed gentleman
Remained seated and refused to give up their seats to white college girls when asked
"A gentleman of this city" who asked them to rise, and "the gentlemen" who seized them; none named

sources.note: Only report: 'THERE WAS NO FIGHT'; two Black men who would not give up seats to college girls on a Fair Grounds car were seized and pulled up from their seats.
quotes: The rumor was that several negroes had refused to give up their seats to white ladies, and had been pushed off the car.
Thereupon the gentlemen seized hold of them and pulled them up from their seats, and there was an end of the matter.
This is the first time that it has been necessary to record any act of rudeness in Raleigh by a negro toward white ladies.
However, these may not have been Raleigh negroes.
